newsitem.title: CROATIA: Serbs rally for rights in last enclave.
newsitem.headline: Serbs rally for rights in last enclave.

text.p: Thousands of Serb protesters, blowing whistles and horns like fellow Serbs demanding democracy in Serbia., marched on Thursday in a separatist enclave in Croatia due to revert to central government rule.

The Eastern Slavonia enclave broke away from Croatia in 1991, opposing Zagreb's drive for independence from federal Yugoslavia. It is now monitored by 5,000 U.N. peacekeeping troops headed by U.S general Jacques Klein.

"Klein, God will punish you,, "Give us our rights" and "We're also made of flesh and blood" were some of the slogans shouted in the raucous but peaceful rally, which echoed the colourful street protests that have rocked Serbia for eight weeks.
But the goals of the demonstrators were quite different.
In Vukovar, they were demanding political autonomy well beyond minority rights guaranteed by Croatian authorities once the region is formally handed back to Zagreb this July.
The crowd, estimated at 5,000, swept through the enclave's main city of Vukovar to the headquarters of the U.N. force to vent their anger and fear.
Olivera Vuletic, 21, a student in Belgrade, returned to the enclave to visit her parents and to "show solidarity with her people here."
"They have nowhere else to go and are getting very frightened over the Croatian and the U.N. proposals. They have no capital or property elsewhere to start again," she said.

The protesters voiced the hope, however faint, that their demonstrations might bring results as in Serbia, where three months of street protests forced President Slobodan Milosevic to finally recognise opposition victories in local elections last November.

But U.N. and Croatian authorities have repeatedly told the Eastern Slavonia Serbs they will get no more than the significant minority rights they agreed to accept in a U.S.-brokered treaty in 1995. It fell short of the "state within a state" status they originally sought.
"We want our basic rights, that is, we must be grouped in one county and the area must be demilitarised on both sides," said Mirjana Stojanovic, a 44-year-old dental assistant.
Croatia, keen to take full control of the enclave and return all non-Serb refugees after the U.N. withdrawal on July 15, will divide it in two counties.

"Everyone demonstrating today desires to stay, but only with this minimal demand (for autonomy). Below this minimum we won't stay and our exodus will be a disgrace for the whole world," Stojanovic said.

U.N. officials blame the agitation for autonomy on misinformation about reintegration spread by some local Serb nationalist leaders. They believe hardline sentiment has waned and most Serbs will peacefully accept Croatian rule in the end.
But most of the protesters winding through Vukovar's streets, still pockmarked with mortar shells from the 1991 fighting, insisted they would leave rather than submit to Croatian authority.
"What I fear most is conflict between individuals here, who used to know each other. Who can guarantee that your former neighbour won't come and kill you overnight?," said Svetislav Vidakovic, 40.
